item.content:encoded:
Climate, Peace and Security Fact Sheet: Somalia

发布源: Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway | 抓取时间: 2026-11-10

Somalia continues to grapple with increasingly severe and frequent climate shocks that impede people’s livelihoods, worsen the existing humanitarian crisis and influence local conflict dynamics over access to natural resources. In November 2025, after four consecutive failed rainy seasons had affected millions of people, the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS) declared a national drought emergency. Strong El Niño conditions are forecast to bring wetter-than-usual conditions during the October–December 2026 deyr rainy season, with a high risk of floods in central and southern Somalia. Some communities experience successive periods of drought and flooding without sufficient time to recover between shocks. These adverse effects of climate change are interacting with a volatile security situation, influenced by political competition and fragmentation, as well as continued clashes with al-Shabab, which contribute to deepening an already dire humanitarian crisis.

The United Nations Security Council recognizes the adverse effects of climate change and natural disasters on Somalia’s humanitarian situation, security and stability. It has called for comprehensive risk assessments and long-term strategies to support stabilization and resilience-building. Integrating environmental and climate considerations into security and development strategies remains crucial for Somalia’s transition towards a more resilient governance structure. Ethiopia, 7 November 2017: Dressed in pink, then Crown Princess Mette-Marit shakes hands with President Mulatu Teshome outside the palace in the capital, Addis Ababa. She and then Crown Prince Haakon are on a state visit with a large business delegation, including Yara, which is set to sign a major agreement to develop a mine in the country's north-eastern Afar region. The aim is to extract potassium sulphate.

"Creating jobs for young people in Ethiopia together. Strategic partnership with Yara," writes Kari H. Partapuoli of the Development Fund of Norway on Twitter.

As part of the mining project, Yara has asked the Development Fund to help renovate a disused local vocational school near the proposed mine. The idea is to give local young people vocational training so they can help build and run the mine.

Norad, the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation, and the Norwegian Embassy in Ethiopia are enthusiastic about the collaboration, a textbook example of what the aid world calls public-private partnerships (PPPs).

item.content:encoded:
ArticlesAnalysisNovember 10, 2026The war that never ended: Norway, Korea and the UN Command

发布源: Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway | 抓取时间: 2026-11-10

In Norwegian defence circles, South Korea is best known as a supplier of military equipment, including a naval support vessel and artillery systems for the Norwegian Army. Far fewer people know that Norway was one of 22 countries that contributed military support after North Korea invaded South Korea in 1950.

Norway’s contribution was NORMASH, the Norwegian Mobile Army Surgical Hospital. According to Lieutenant General Scott Winter, deputy commander of the United Nations Command, Korea, the hospital treated more than 90,000 patients and performed some 14,000 surgeries.

“It’s certainly not forgotten by the Koreans,” says Winter.

Winter is an officer in the Australian Army and Deputy Commander of the United Nations Command in Korea. He explains that the 1953 armistice was designed to last for weeks or months. The war never formally ended, and 18 of the original 22 nations remain active members of the command.

In conversation with Senior Defence Analyst Per Erik Solli (NUPI), Winter describes how the command is led today. He also covers its access to seven bases in Japan and the maritime operations that enforce UN sanctions against North Korea.

We research law as an instrument of social change.

We are at the forefront of research on how law and legal institutions work, and the strategic use of law as a political tool (lawfare).

As a key partner in theCentre on Law and SocialTransformation, we are developing new and better methods for assessing effects of lawfare.

We study how political institutions, political processes  and political action shape and are shaped by democracy and rights, economic outcomes and social development.

Rule of law, civil liberties and basic political rights are under threat in countries worldwide.

Our research focuses on the growing pressure against democratic institutions in Africa. We have cooperated closely with African partners for decades and have extensive fieldwork experience.

Our research holds high academic quality and provides concrete input to actors engaged in bilateral work, and to donors and activists navigating the shrinking space for civil society.
